imperative

im-PER-uh-tiv -- stress on the second syllable, PER. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Imperative is of vital or crucial importance.

With the storm just hours away, it was imperative that every boat in the harbor be secured.

Example

The mountain guide checks the forecast, sees the blizzard closing in, and tells the climbers it is imperative that they descend now -- not after lunch, not in an hour, now.

Descending immediately is not optional or merely wise -- it is a matter of vital, non-negotiable importance. Imperative describes what is absolutely crucial, what must be done above all else.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

essential: Essential means so important that a thing cannot succeed without it -- water is essential to life. Imperative adds command and urgency on top: an imperative step is not just needed, it must be acted on, because everything depends on it. Essential names a requirement; imperative issues an order.

compulsory: Compulsory means required by a rule or an authority -- school attendance is compulsory because the law says so. Imperative needs no rulebook: something is imperative because the situation itself demands it, with everything riding on the outcome. Compulsory points to a rule; imperative points to the stakes.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

optional: left to one's own choice

trivial: of little value or importance

Where it sits · how much depends on it — pressing → imperative → vital

pressing vs. imperative: Pressing is urgent but lighter than imperative -- a pressing task wants your attention today, while an imperative one must be done, full stop, because everything depends on it.

vital vs. imperative: Vital can weigh even more than imperative: an imperative step must be taken for the plan to succeed, while a vital one carries the force of life itself -- lose it, and the whole effort dies.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — im- (in-)

prefix — im- (in-): in, upon (Latin)

root — per(a)-

root — per(a)-: to make ready, to arrange (Latin parare)

suffix — -ative

suffix — -ative: relating to; having the quality of (Latin -ativus)

Put it together

Put it together: Imperative descends from Latin imperare, 'to command' -- built from in- ('upon') and parare ('to make ready'): a commander literally made others ready for action. Something imperative carries that commanding force: it is so vitally important that it feels like an order no one may refuse.

Word Choice

Imperative appears in two main frames: before a noun ('an imperative need for reform') and, most often, in 'It is imperative that...' followed by a demand ('It is imperative that all passengers remain seated'). It outranks 'important' and even 'urgent' -- reserve it for necessities on which everything else depends.
